Package hadur2.core.physics

Class BattleField

java.lang.Object
hadur2.core.physics.BattleField
public class BattleField extends Object
The battle field's walls, as seen by a robot's centre, and the geometry that depends on them: clamping a point into the field, how far a target can move before a wall stops it (two of the gun's and the surf's KNN features), and wall smoothing.

A robot is a 36 × 36 px square, so its centre can never come closer than 18 px to a wall. rectangle is the field shrunk by those 18 px on every side: the set of legal centre positions. Every method here works on centres against that rectangle, not on the field's own edges.

Coordinates are Robocode's: the origin is the bottom-left corner, +y is north (up), and angles are radians with 0 north and growing clockwise, so a point at angle a and distance d from p is (p.x + sin(a) d, p.y + cos(a) d).

One instance is made per battle from the field size and shared by the movement predictor, the waves, the guns, the surf and the melee brain. It is immutable.

    • translateToField

      public Point2D.Double translateToField(Point2D.Double p)
      Clamps a point into the area a robot's centre can occupy, [18, width - 18] × [18, height - 18]. Used where a prediction ran through a wall (the precise escape angle's end point, the melee's candidate points) and the answer must be a place a robot could really be.
      Parameters:
      p - the point, in field coordinates (not modified)
      Returns:
      a new point, p moved onto the nearest legal position if it was outside

    • orbitalWallDistance

      public double orbitalWallDistance(Point2D.Double sourceLocation, Point2D.Double targetLocation, double bulletPower, int direction)
      How far the target can orbit the source, at its current distance, before its centre leaves the field: the gun and the surf read it as a KNN feature (a wave's "wall distance" forward and reverse), so that a target pinned against a wall is not expected to escape the way one in open field would.

      The answer is in units of the classic maximum escape angle, asin(8 / bulletSpeed): the widest angle a target at full speed (8 px/tick) can cover, seen from the source, before a bullet of this power reaches it. So 1.0 means the wall is exactly one escape angle away along the orbit, and the value is directly comparable with a guess factor. The circle is walked in steps of 1% of the escape angle, up to 2 escape angles; 2.0 means no wall within that.

      Parameters:
      sourceLocation - where the bullet is fired from
      targetLocation - the target's centre; its distance from the source is the orbit's radius
      bulletPower - the bullet's power, which sets its speed and so the escape angle
      direction - +1 to orbit clockwise, -1 counter-clockwise (a wave's orbit direction, or its reverse)
      Returns:
      the wall's distance along the orbit, as a multiple of the escape angle, in [0, 2]

    • directToWallDistance

      public double directToWallDistance(Point2D.Double targetLocation, double distance, double heading, double bulletPower)
      How far the target can drive straight along heading, at full speed, before its centre leaves the field, as a share of the bullet's flight time: 1.0 means it would reach the wall just as the bullet arrives. The path is walked a tick (8 px) at a time for up to two flight times; 2.0 means no wall within that. Nothing in the core calls it at present.
      Parameters:
      targetLocation - the target's centre
      distance - the bullet's flight distance, in px, which sets its flight time
      heading - the direction the target would drive, in radians
      bulletPower - the bullet's power, which sets its speed
      Returns:
      ticks to the wall divided by the bullet's flight time in ticks, in [0, 2]

    • wallSmoothing

      public double wallSmoothing(Point2D.Double startLocation, double startAngle, int orientation, double wallStick)
      Wall smoothing: bends a desired heading just enough that a robot driving along it slides along a wall instead of running into it. Movement calls it on every heading it is about to drive, so a surfing or orbiting robot turns smoothly along walls and never loses speed (and energy) to a wall hit.

      The test is a "stick" of length wallStick held out from the robot along the heading. While the stick's tip is outside rectangle, the heading is replaced by one that points at the offending wall and then rotated away from it by exactly the angle that puts the tip back on the wall line: if the robot is adjacent px from the wall, a stick at angle θ from the wall's normal reaches wallStick × cos θ toward it, so θ = acos(adjacent / wallStick). A further 0.0005 rad keeps the tip just inside. Near a corner the new heading can poke through the other wall, so the loop repeats, at most 25 times. A robot already outside the rectangle (negative adjacent) is steered back in, lengthening the stick if it is shorter than the overshoot so that acos stays defined.

      Parameters:
      startLocation - the robot's centre
      startAngle - the heading it wants to drive, in radians
      orientation - which way to rotate off a wall: +1 clockwise, -1 counter-clockwise (the direction the robot is orbiting in)
      wallStick - the stick's length, in px: longer turns off a wall sooner and more gently
      Returns:
      the smoothed heading, in radians; startAngle unchanged when the robot is more than wallStick from both walls
